pages.text: On a hot afternoon, Afua’s phone buzzed with a photo from her cousin Ruth in London. It showed a wide, grey river, and in the water, a round, whiskered head. “A seal!” Ruth wrote. “In the middle of the city, in the River Thames.” Afua stared. Beside her school, the little stream was brown and choked with plastic. “Seals,” she whispered. “In a city river?”
sentences: On a hot afternoon, Afua’s phone buzzed with a photo from her cousin Ruth in London.
It showed a wide, grey river, and in the water, a round, whiskered head.
“A seal!” Ruth wrote.
“In the middle of the city, in the River Thames.” Afua stared.
Beside her school, the little stream was brown and choked with plastic.
“Seals,” she whispered.
“In a city river?”
pages.alt: A girl looks at a phone showing a seal in a river while a polluted stream flows behind her.

pages.text: Mr Fordjour, the science teacher, smiled when she told him. “That river has a hard history,” he said. “In 1957, scientists at the Natural History Museum in London said that large parts of the Thames were biologically dead. The sewage and waste of a growing city had used up the oxygen in the water, and almost nothing could live in it.” Afua’s mouth fell open. “Dead,” she said. “A whole river?”
sentences: Mr Fordjour, the science teacher, smiled when she told him.
“That river has a hard history,” he said.
“In 1957, scientists at the Natural History Museum in London said that large parts of the Thames were biologically dead.
The sewage and waste of a growing city had used up the oxygen in the water, and almost nothing could live in it.” Afua’s mouth fell open.
“Dead,” she said.
“A whole river?”
pages.alt: A teacher points to a model river with a skull sign beside the dirtiest stretch.

pages.text: “It took decades,” said Mr Fordjour. “The city built better sewage treatment, and industries were made to stop dumping waste. Slowly, oxygen returned, and so did the animals. Reports now record seals, eels and well over a hundred species of fish.” He paused. “But I want you to hear the full truth. The river is better, not perfect.”
sentences: “It took decades,” said Mr Fordjour.
“The city built better sewage treatment, and industries were made to stop dumping waste.
Slowly, oxygen returned, and so did the animals.
Reports now record seals, eels and well over a hundred species of fish.” He paused.
“But I want you to hear the full truth.
The river is better, not perfect.”
pages.alt: A teacher explains a diagram of sewage treatment with fish returning to the river in the picture.

pages.text: He wrote three problems on the board. “Old sewers still overflow into the river when it rains hard. Nitrates, which come from waste and fertiliser, have increased. And the river is warming with the climate. A huge new tunnel was built to catch most of the overflow, but the work is not finished, and the number of fish species has slipped since the early 1990s, for reasons scientists do not fully know.” Afua wrote it all down.

A huge new tunnel was built to catch most of the overflow, but the work is not finished, and the number of fish species has slipped since the early 1990s, for reasons scientists do not fully know.” Afua wrote it all down.

pages.text: “So what do we learn?” asked Mr Fordjour. A boy said, “It can be done.” A girl said, “It takes a long time.” Afua said, “It is never finished. You have to keep looking after it.” Mr Fordjour nodded. “Exactly. Clean-up is not a single event. It takes laws, money, science, patience and ordinary people who refuse to give up.”

pages.alt: Students sit in a circle answering their teacher’s question with notebooks open.

pages.text: After school, Afua and her friends walked to the little stream. “It is only brown because of what we put in it,” she said. “If London could bring back a river, we can start with ours.” They agreed on small steps: a litter patrol, a weekly check of the drain and a letter to their Assembly about the dumping upstream. “We may not see the seals,” said Afua, “but someone will.”

pages.alt: Students pick up plastic along a brown stream with notebooks and bags.

pages.text: Afua wrote to her cousin, with her address and the date at the top. “House 6, School Road, Cape Coast. 7th May, 2027. Dear Ruth, I hope you are well. Thank you for the photograph of the seal. It made me think about our own stream, which is dirty but not hopeless. I learned that your river took many years to recover, and that it still needs care. In the same way, we can start small. Please send me more news of the Thames. Yours ever, Afua.”
sentences: Afua wrote to her cousin, with her address and the date at the top.
“House 6, School Road, Cape Coast.
7th May, 2027.
Dear Ruth, I hope you are well.
Thank you for the photograph of the seal.
It made me think about our own stream, which is dirty but not hopeless.
I learned that your river took many years to recover, and that it still needs care.
In the same way, we can start small.
Please send me more news of the Thames.
Yours ever, Afua.”
pages.alt: A girl writes a letter at a desk beside a photo of a seal and a small jar of clean water.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: this informal letter compares two places. Afua used linking phrases such as “in the same way” and “but not hopeless”, and she gave a reason for her feeling. Notice the address, date, “Dear Ruth” and “Yours ever”. When you compare in writing, say what is similar, what is different and what you learned. The end.
